source.title: Steering the CensorShip: Uncovering Representation Vectors for LLM "Thought" Control

record.tranche_reason: The study finds a refusal–compliance vector and intervenes on it, measuring refusal on user requests. Its method differs from the original: it uses weighted refusal/compliance activations and activation steering at a selected layer, rather than the original difference-in-means direction and all-layer ablation.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports refusal probabilities before and after steering and is included. The paper also reports correlations and detection accuracy used to select or compare vectors (Tables 3 and 4); these are not behavioral outcomes of applying the claim's direction. Table 2 reports refusal and thought-suppression rates in reasoning models, but does not apply a refusal–compliance vector to them. Those measurements and the separate thought-suppression steering result are recorded as findings that fit no version. The joint refusal-and-no-thinking metric in Table 2 and subject-level breakdowns in Table 6 are left out under the row limit.
record.test_reason: The study extracts a single refusal–compliance vector (weighted mean difference against a grey-zone reference) and steers it at one selected layer. It reports refusal probabilities going down at λ = −1 and up at λ = 1 across 8 chat/instruct models (Table 1). This is a different method aimed at V1's question of whether one direction causally mediates refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors assume censorship lies on a one-dimensional refusal–compliance subspace. They conclude that their vector both detects censorship (projections correlate with refusal scores) and gives fine-grained control of it in instruction models. They also conclude that DeepSeek-R1 distills show an additional 'thought suppression' censorship dimension. A separate vector steers this dimension, and negative multiples restore reasoning. They present the method as neutral, able to weaken or strengthen censorship.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weighted refusal/compliance activation means with a grey-zone reference and neutralization-plus-steering at one selected layer. It does not use the original difference-in-means direction or ablate it at every layer.
record.method_sensitivity: Effect varies by model and benchmark; at λ = −1 refusal remains higher on some conditions, including Qwen-7B-Chat on JAILBREAKBENCH and XSTEST unsafe. For reasoning-model thought suppression, the sign and magnitude of λ change the next-token probabilities.

fits_no_version.finding: DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B/7B/32B) skip reasoning ('<think>\n\n</think>') on 60–75% of CCP-sensitive prompts versus ≤5% on harmful/harmless prompts. A separate thought-suppression vector steers the stop/continue-thinking token probabilities. In Example D.8, removing thought suppression (λ = −1.5) still yields an explicit refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-distilled models carry a censorship direction for skipping chain-of-thought that is distinct from, and can dissociate from, the refusal decision.

record.problems: The refusal-rate outcomes use the WildGuard moderation model and its token probabilities; the paper notes that refusal estimates from string matching may not capture true refusal probability. The capability evaluation is limited to JudgeLM ratings on benign tasks for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the intervention results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's joint (refuse∧¬think)% values and Table 6's subject-level censorship percentages are not included because the 60-row limit was reached after preserving separate model, prompt-type, and metric results. Tables 3 and 4 report vector selection or method-comparison metrics rather than behavioral outcomes of applying the claim's direction, so they were excluded under the gate rule.

untested.parts: The original difference-in-means direction and all-layer directional ablation (the intervention here is projection removal plus λ-scaled addition at one layer, relative to a grey-zone reference). Standard capability benchmarks. Capability retention on any model other than Qwen2.5-7B.
No refusal–compliance vector is applied to the DeepSeek-R1 distills. Only a separate thought-suppression vector is steered, and its measured outcome is next-token probability, not refusal rate.

missing.what: λ sweep from −1 to 1 (step 0.2) of refusal and harmful-response probability on JailbreakBench, SorryBench and XSTest-unsafe for all 8 models. At λ = 0 (projection removed, akin to single-layer ablation to the grey-zone reference) refusal is about 0.5, not removed. Harmful-response probability rises as λ becomes more negative.
missing.locator: Figure 1; Appendix B.2 Figure 4; Section 3.4 text

missing.what: Harmfulness probabilities of uncensored outputs at λ = −1 for Llama3.1-8B (0.45–0.68) and Qwen2.5-7B (0.56–0.71). Llama3.1 XSTest-unsafe reaches refusal 0.07 at λ = −1.4. These show compliance is substantive, not just absent refusal.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 values are all verified correct. The intervention is not the original method: it uses weighted mean difference with a grey-zone reference point, a single layer chosen by RMSE/correlation (excluding the last 20% of layers), and projection removal plus λ-scaled addition applied at every token. λ = −1 is therefore stronger than pure ablation. Refusal is measured by WildGuard token probabilities with 5 samples and top-p 0.8. No uncertainty is reported. Tables 3–4 (layer selection, comparison with Lee et al.) are correctly excluded as selection or method-comparison metrics. Table 2 rows correctly carry no version, since no refusal direction is applied to the reasoning models. Qwen-7B and Yi-XU partial labels follow the paper's own note of lower effectiveness. The paper says larger negative λ may reduce refusal further.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the original difference-in-means direction, ablation at every layer, or broad retention of other abilities. It tests steering at a selected layer; output quality is checked only on benign requests for Qwen2.5-7B.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
The study does not test whether refusal is represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions. Its separate thought-suppression vector concerns a different behavior.
Harmful-response probability is measured, but the study does not test whether a harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
No transfer test across languages, base/instruct variants, or model variants.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.
The study measures refusal in reasoning models and steers a distinct thought-suppression behavior, but does not test whether a refusal–compliance direction mediates their refusals.

tranche.reason: The study uses a different direction-finding method: a weighted refusal-vs-compliance mean difference against a grey-zone reference, not harmful-minus-harmless difference in means.
